\title{Explore Once, Evaluate Many: Multiple Policy Evaluation for Stochastic Linear Bandits}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}%
We study how to evaluate $K$ target policies simultaneously
in stochastic contextual bandits with linear reward structure.
Given a known $d$-dimensional feature map and reward-free
access to policy queries, we propose PRISMA (Policy evaluation through Regularized
Information Sharing and Mixture Allocation), an algorithm
that estimates every target policy's value to accuracy
$\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
The algorithm uses
$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(
\frac{(L^2S^2+\beta^2)(1\vee\rho^\star)}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot \log(K)
\right)$ context draws and reward observations,
where $\rho^\star\le d$ is an instance-dependent measure
of the difficulty of designing a shared sampling distribution.
Here, $L$, $S$, and $\beta$ bound the feature norm,
reward parameter norm, and reward noise, respectively,
and the suppressed factors are logarithmic in
$K$, $d$, and $1/\delta$.
Our method combines reward-free planning, a regularized
sampling design, and a single ridge regression estimator
shared across all target policies.
An adaptive doubling procedure selects the regularization
scale without knowledge of $\rho^\star$.
The guarantees require no numerical lower bound on
second-moment eigenvalues and have no explicit dependence
on the cardinalities of the context and action spaces.
Policy-query costs are accounted for separately,
with $K$ queries per shared planning context.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

We studied simultaneous policy evaluation in stochastic
contextual bandits with linear reward structure.
Our results show that reward-free planning and a shared
sampling design yield instance-dependent guarantees
without explicit dependence on the cardinalities of
the context and action spaces or a numerical lower
bound on second-moment eigenvalues.

A natural direction is to extend these techniques to
linear MDPs and more general function approximation settings.
In these settings, an additional challenge is that
the policies influence the distributions of future states,
so feature moments cannot be estimated directly from
a shared policy-independent context distribution.

An open question is whether $\rho\opt$ captures the
intrinsic difficulty of evaluation in the linear setting.
Our analysis provides an upper bound in terms of this
quantity, but does not establish its necessity.
Matching lower bounds would help determine when mixtures
of target policies achieve the optimal evaluation cost
and whether more general sampling strategies can improve
upon them.
